Long life has a price Repair and renew • The cell cycle and stem cells let us outlive most of our cells. • Without repair and renewal, our lifetimes would be much shorter. The price • We carry cells poised to divide. • Their behavior is balanced on a fulcrum of signaling molecules, gene regulation and phosphorylation. When such a balanced system fails, it can fail catastrophically. Cancer is an example: about 1 in 4 people in Europe and North America die of it.

A well-run society of cells Work for the greater good Each cell does what it does for the organism. Listen to signals Cell communication and signal transduction keep each cell in step with what the body needs. Divide only when needed New cells of its type must be required. Live as long as needed Undergo apoptosis once the need has passed. Keep your identity Maintain cellular and biochemical character. Stay in place Remain where the cell belongs.

Cancer breaks the rules One cell misbehaves In trillions of cells, a single rule-breaker is usually no big deal It enters the cell cycle The cell begins dividing Instability is inherited Daughter cells pass on the same asocial behavior A selfish mass forms Crowds, pushes on and destroys nearby tissue Cancer: a relentlessly expanding clone of abnormal cells, each putting its own survival first.

Three defining behaviors Proliferative Divide uncontrollably, in defiance of normal constraints. Invasive Move into other tissues and colonize regions reserved for other cell types. Metastatic Spread from one organ system to another. These properties are passed to daughter cells, and the combination makes cancer so devastating: rapid growth wherever it wants.

Benign, malignant, metastatic Benign Proliferates but does not invade. A rapidly growing mass that stays localized and can usually be removed completely by surgery. Malignant A tumor is malignant only if it can invade surrounding tissues. Metastatic Cells have invaded or reached a blood or lymph supply line, so they can leave the primary site.

How metastasis happens Invade neighboring tissue Cells leave the primary tumor Enter blood or lymph Malignant cells reach the circulation Travel through the body Blood or lymph carries them elsewhere Secondary tumor forms Cells land, divide and grow Secondary tumors keep the properties of the primary tumor: they stay rapidly dividing and invasive.

What is cancer? Cancer A group of more than 100 diseases marked by uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells. It begins when a single cell escapes the regulation of its own division. Normal control Genes switch on and off to set when and how fast a cell divides, when it stops, and when it dies. Cancer results when these controls are lost. The name: 'cancer' is Latin for crab, since it spreads from a primary tumor to distant sites.

Normal versus cancerous growth Normal division Cell divides only when needed Damage is detected Repair, or apoptosis if beyond repair Tissue stays balanced Cancer cell division First mutation More mutations accumulate Apoptosis and growth controls lost Uncontrolled growth: tumor

Cancer is a disease of cellular mutation Mutations can happen in many ways • Anything that raises mutation rates raises cancer risk, including smoking. • Mutations also arise spontaneously, so cancer cannot be fully eradicated. • It is fundamentally a disease born from inside us. Somatic, not germline • A germline mutation is present in every cell of the organism. • An organism of entirely unregulated cells would not be viable or survive to birth. • So cancer arises from somatic mutations. Inherited cancer risk exists, but it works by making a somatic second hit easier.

DNA copying is accurate, but scale matters 1 in 109-1010 bases copied is wrong, even with no environmental effect ~1016 cell divisions occur in a human body over a lifetime ~107 - 109 separate mutations arise in every single gene over a lifetime One of the most accurate processes in nature still makes mistakes at this scale, so the surprise is that we do not all develop cancer in infancy.

Why we do not all get cancer early Randomness protects us • Cancer rarely results from a single mutation. • It needs a specific combination of mutations in one cell. • A cancer cell must be proliferative and invasive, which takes several mutations. Time makes it likely • Such combinations are rare in a single cell. • Enough time and enough combinations eventually produce one. • This, more than anything else, is why cancer is a disease of old age.

Genetic instability speeds progression Repair lost Mutations deactivate DNA repair enzymes or DNA proofreading. Checkpoints bypassed Mutations bypass cell-cycle checkpoints, such as p53. Mitosis defective Mutations damage the machinery needed for mitosis. Result: large-scale chromosomal mutations, so the entire genome can be radically altered. This is the biggest cancer risk.

Tumors evolve: natural selection at work Rapid division Random mutations arise Selection favors the best survivors Super-cells out- compete normal cells Not crippling, but empowering • The mutations make 'super-cells', the opposite of crippled cells. • Rapid division gives the potential for rapid evolution. • Evolution then works against the patient. Super-cell traits • Rapid division • Invasiveness • Ability to attract a blood supply • Ability to degrade the extracellular matrix • Ability to enter blood or lymph

Six acquired advantages of cancer cells 1 No signal needed No longer require signals from other cells to thrive, e.g., Ras locked active. 2 No default apoptosis Normal cells sacrifice themselves; cancer cells, with no p53 or DNA-damage block, do not. 3 Immortal Never cease dividing, while normal cells do. 4 Genetically unstable Chromosome mutations accumulate. 5 Abnormally invasive Lack of cadherin and other junction proteins lets cells slip away. 6 Survive anywhere Adhere to, survive in and divide in foreign tissues; this is metastasis.
Cancer-associated mutations converge on key cellular pathways Different tumours alter different combinations of pathways.

Two classes of cancer genes Oncogene: gain of function, genetically dominant Normal cell: proto-oncogene One activating mutation Oncogene active: excess survival and proliferation Tumor suppressor gene: loss of function, genetically recessive Normal cell: two good copies First hit: no effect Second hit: gene lost, excess proliferation Oncogene = protein activity itself causes disease. Tumor suppressor = absence of a protective protein causes disease.

Inherited predisposition: the two-hit logic Why carriers are at higher risk • Two healthy alleles: both must be mutated, so risk is about p squared. • One mutant allele inherited: only the remaining good allele must mutate, so risk is about p. • Inherited risk is therefore much higher. 0% 10% 20% 30% 40% 50% 60% 70% 30 35 40 45 50 55 60 65 70 75 80 Age (years) BRCA1/2 mutations: breast cancer risk by age (%) Carriers Noncarriers

In most tumors both oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes are mutated. The Warburg effect: aerobic glycolysis Normal cell Glucose Pyruvate Mitochondria: oxidative phosphorylation About 30 ATP per glucose Cancer cell Glucose, taken up at a high rate Pyruvate Converted to lactate 2 ATP per glucose, plus lactate Otto Warburg observed in the 1920s that tumors turn glucose into lactate even when oxygen is plentiful.

Why choose the less efficient route? Building blocks Glycolytic intermediates feed synthesis of nucleotides, amino acids and lipids needed to build new cells. Speed over efficiency Glycolysis makes ATP quickly, trading yield per glucose for rate. Acidic surroundings Lactate lowers the pH around the tumor, aiding invasion and dampening immune cells. Mitochondria still work Most tumors also use oxidative metabolism, so the picture is flexible, not all-or- none.

Using the Warburg effect in the clinic Inject FDG, a glucose analog Radiolabeled with fluorine-18 Cells take it up Through glucose transporters (GLUT) Hexokinase traps it It cannot continue down glycolysis PET scan shows bright spots High glucose uptake marks tumors Why it is hard • Brain, heart and immune T cells also need glucose • Tumors adapt using other fuels • No diet has been proven to cure cancer FDG-fluorodeoxyglucose

Case study: colorectal cancer The disease Cancer of the epithelial lining of the colon and rectum. Typically associated with old age and not genetic. Hereditary cases A small proportion show predisposition, pointing to a tumor suppressor gene. In one family it is a DNA repair enzyme; in another, hundreds to thousands of polyps form early, due to the APC gene. Two-hit pattern Carriers are heterozygous; cancer develops when the wild- type allele mutates. In over 60% of other cases, both APC alleles are lost in the tumor but present in healthy tissue. APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) is an inhibitory protein which blocks a cell signalling pathway responsible for cell proliferation in the gut
A signal that promotes cell growth called Wnt

APC and the Wnt pathway No Wnt signal: proliferation genes off Receptor inactive APC complex active Beta-catenin degraded TCF inactive: genes OFF Wnt signal present, or APC mutated: gut cells proliferate Receptor active APC complex inhibited Beta-catenin stable TCF active: genes ON A signal that promotes cell growth called Wnt

Cancer treatment targets the tumour and its biological vulnerabilities Surgery Remove localised tumour when feasible Radiotherapy Damage DNA in a defined treatment field Chemotherapy Systemic drugs that impair cell division or survival Targeted therapy Inhibit a specific altered protein or pathway Immunotherapy Enhance or restore anti-tumour immune activity Treatment is selected according to cancer type, stage, molecular features and patient factors.

Chemotherapy and targeted therapy work in different ways CHEMOTHERAPY Often targets processes used by many dividing cells. Can affect tumour cells and some normal tissues with high turnover, contributing to adverse effects. Affect normal cells that have high proliferation TARGETED THERAPY Designed to inhibit a defined molecular target or pathway. Requires the tumour to depend on that target or carry a relevant biomarker. Resistance can emerge through pathway reactivation or new alterations. “Targeted” does not mean side-effect-free, and not every tumour has an actionable target.

Radiotherapy exploits DNA damage—but normal tissue also matters X Tumour cells Treatment planning Dose and beam geometry aim to maximise tumour control while limiting exposure to nearby normal tissue. Radiation-induced DNA lesions can prevent tumour cells from completing replication and division; repair capacity influences response.

Molecular profiling can guide precision oncology 1 Obtain tumour sample 2 Profile DNA / RNA / proteins 3 Identify actionable alteration 4 Select evidence- based therapy A molecular alteration is clinically useful only when it predicts response to an available intervention with supporting evidence.

Other modern strategies Starve the tumor Block formation of new blood vessels that feed it, impeding growth. Vaccines Let your own immune system recognize unique features of cancer cells and fight them as it would an infection. Targeted drugs Block the signal-transduction cascade that drives cell proliferation. Cancer is deadly and is not going away, but good cell biology shows how cells should work, laying the groundwork for fixing what is broken.

Infectious diseases in the ancient world • Disease has shaped human history for as long as we have records • Infectious diseases shaped population size, settlement, warfare, trade and social organisation. • Ancient art and texts describe plagues and skin eruptions such as pustules • Nobody could see the cause, so explanations were religious or supernatural • Crowded settlements, trade and war helped diseases spread

Infectious diseases in the ancient world Why outbreaks mattered • High mortality could alter the size and age structure of communities. • Outbreaks disrupted food production, trade, travel and military campaigns. • Without microbiology, diagnosis relied on symptoms, patterns and observation. • Historical records rarely provide modern laboratory confirmation.

Epidemic vs Endemic vs Pandemic • Endemic: consistently present in one region, rates predictable (e.g., malaria) • Epidemic: unexpected rise in cases in a specific area (e.g., polio) • Pandemic: growth is exponential and crosses regions (e.g., COVID-19, Spanish flu) • The difference is how many, where and how fast These terms describe patterns and geographic spread—not different types of pathogen.
Epidemic vs Endemic vs Pandemic – factors needed to classify

Epidemic vs endemic vs pandemic EPIDEMIC An unexpected increase in cases above the baseline in a particular population, place and time. Example: a local outbreak of polio. ENDEMIC A disease that is consistently present in a population or region. The level may vary over time. Example: malaria in some regions. PANDEMIC An epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents. Geographic spread—not exponential growth alone—is the defining feature. Examples: COVID-19 and the 1918 influenza pandemic.

Plague of Justinian 6th century Black Death 14th century Smallpox Across centuries 1918 influenza 1918–1920 COVID-19 2019 onward A history of major pandemics Interpreting historical estimates Reported death tolls are uncertain: population records, diagnostic criteria and attribution of deaths differ across eras.

• Plague of Justinian and the Black Death: tens of millions dead • 1918 influenza: about 50 million deaths worldwide • HIV/AIDS and COVID-19 in our own lifetime • Death tolls fall with better sanitation, vaccines and antibiotics, but new pandemics still appear A history of major pandemics https://www.visualcapitalist.com/history-of-pandemics-deadliest/

Death toll: what does it tell us? • Transmission: How efficiently and widely does the infection spread? • Severity: What fraction of infected people develop severe disease or die? • Duration and scale: How long does the outbreak last, and how many people are exposed? A high death toll does not, by itself, mean a pathogen is highly transmissible.

R0: how infectious is a disease? • R0 (R-naught) is the average number of people each sick person infects • R0 > 1: outbreak grows; R0 < 1: it dies out • Typical values: flu about 1.5, Ebola about 2, measles 12-18 • Vaccination, masks and isolation all work by lowering R0

R0: how infectious is a disease? Illustrative branching pattern when R₀ is approximately 2 R₀ is a population average, not a prediction for every infected person. It differs from the time-varying effective reproduction number, Rₜ. WHAT R₀ MEANS The average number of secondary infections generated by one infectious person in a fully susceptible population, under specified conditions. HOW TO READ IT R₀ > 1: transmission can grow R₀ < 1: transmission tends to decline R₀ = 1: cases may remain roughly steady

The search for causes • Early explanations: supernatural forces, climate, soil, air, bad omens • The idea of miasma: disease carried by foul air • Reasonable guesses without a way to test them • Understanding needed observation, then instruments 14

Early epidemiology: Hippocrates • Called the father of modern medicine • Argued for natural causes and the idea of contagion, not magic • Observed seasonal patterns in specific diseases • Linked disease to poorly cooked food; saw fever and swelling as part of the body's response 15

Microbes as disease-causing agents • Girolamo Fracastoro proposed invisible, self replicating "seeds" of disease (1500s) • Transmission by direct contact, air and objects • Described syphilis and foot-and-mouth disease in cattle • A correct idea without proof: nobody had yet seen a microbe 16

The first microscope: Leeuwenhoek • Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, 1600s: founder of microbiology • Ground single lenses and observed living "animalcules" in water and saliva • First time humans saw bacteria and protozoa • A new measurement tool opened a new field

Edward Jenner and the first vaccine • Edward Jenner (1749-1823): father of immunology • Variolation: giving a little real virus to prevent a worse case, but risky • Milkmaids who caught mild cowpox seemed protected from smallpox • 1796: cowpox material protected a boy from smallpox, the first vaccine 18

The first clinical trial • Jenner tested a prediction: cowpox first, then deliberate challenge with smallpox • The boy stayed healthy: the vaccine worked • Basic ingredients of a trial: intervention, outcome, comparison • Modern trials also need consent, controls and ethics review 19

Louis Pasteur: the father of microbiology Louis Pasteur (1822–1895) Germ theory Microorganisms can be responsible for fermentation and infectious disease. Pasteurization Controlled heating reduces harmful microbes and spoilage organisms. Vaccination Attenuated microbes can induce protection against later infection. Scientific impact Experiments replaced speculation with testable explanations. Key idea: microbial growth comes from pre-existing microbial contamination—not from non-living broth.

Louis Pasteur: the father of microbiology • Louis Pasteur (1822-1895): disproved spontaneous generation • Established the germ theory of disease • Discovered microbial fermentation and invented pasteurization • Developed vaccines against cholera, rabies and anthrax The germ theory of disease is the scientific principle stating that specific infectious diseases are caused by microscopic living organisms—such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa—that invade and multiply within a host body

Pasteur's swan-neck flask • Broth in a flask with a long S-shaped neck • Air could enter, but dust and microbes were trapped in the bend • The broth stayed clear; tilt the flask and it turned cloudy • Conclusion: access to air alone did not cause growth; contamination by microorganisms did. 5

Vaccine development • Pasteur found that weakened microbes could protect, an idea now called attenuation • Chicken cholera, then anthrax in sheep, then rabies • Rabies vaccine used on a child in 1885 • Idea: show the immune system a safe version of the threat 6

Robert Koch and the identification of pathogens Robert Koch (1843–1910) Robert Koch (1843-1910): father of bacteriology Developed methods to isolate and grow bacteria in pure culture. Linked specific microorganisms to diseases, including tuberculosis and anthrax. Received the 1905 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on tuberculosis. Why it mattered A reproducible link between a microorganism and a disease made causation testable.

Fleming and penicillin • Alexander Fleming (1881-1955) discovered lysozyme and penicillin • Mould on a plate killed nearby bacteria • First broadly effective antibiotic; Florey and Chain mass produced and all three won the Nobel Prize 1945 • Antibiotics fight bacterial infections in people and animals 9

Antibiotic resistance • Bacteria evolve under antibiotic pressure • Antibiotic exposure suppresses susceptible bacteria; resistant ones survive and reproduce. • Fleming himself warned about misuse • A global threat: new antibiotics are discovered slowly Resistance is a property of bacteria—not the patient. Inappropriate use increases selection pressure.

Microbes are everywhere • Invisible to the naked eye and omnipresent • Many sizes and shapes, useful and harmful • Exist in huge numbers: they outnumber all other species • Make up most of the living matter on the planet - by number, diversity and number of species, microbes dominate 12

Normal microbiota and the host • We carry trillions of microbes on skin, gut and mouth: our microbiota • They help with digestion, vitamins and training the immune system • They crowd out pathogens (competitive exclusion) • Imbalance (e.g., after antibiotics) can allow infection

Reservoirs and vectors • Reservoir: where a pathogen normally lives (animals, soil, water) • Vector: arthropods such as fleas, ticks and mosquitoes • Mechanical vector: carries pathogens on its feet • Biological vector: the pathogen replicates in the vector 14

Portals of entry: how pathogens enter the body Skin Intact skin is an effective barrier. Entry may occur through cuts, bites, burns or hair follicles. Respiratory mucosa Inhaled droplets or aerosols can expose the airways; influenza is one example. Gastrointestinal mucosa Ingestion of contaminated food or water can transmit pathogens such as Vibrio cholerae. Urogenital / conjunctival mucosa Sexual exposure can transmit HIV; adenoviruses can infect the conjunctiva.

Blood-borne and vertical transmission Blood-borne exposure Transmission can occur through contaminated needles, unsafe transfusion or blood contact. Vector inoculation Some arthropods introduce pathogens into skin or blood during feeding. Vertical transmission A pathogen passes from parent to child during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding. Example: HIV HIV can be transmitted through blood, sexual exposure and perinatal routes; prevention and treatment reduce risk.

What are bacteria? • Large group of unicellular microorganisms • Have cell walls but lack organelles and an organised nucleus • Some cause disease; most do not Bacteria are diverse: many are harmless or beneficial, while some cause infectious disease.

What are bacteria? • Large group of unicellular organisms with cell walls • No organelles and no organised nucleus • Found in soil, water, air, and on and inside us • Some cause disease; most are harmless or helpful 2

Bacterial structure • Cell wall: gives shape and protection • Plasma membrane: controls what enters and leaves • Nucleoid: circular DNA with no membrane; plasmids carry extra genes • Ribosomes make protein; flagella move the cell; pili attach 3

A motor that lives inside you • The flagellum is driven by a rotary motor in the cell envelope • Powered by a proton flow across the membrane, not by ATP directly • Spins at thousands of rpm and can reverse direction • Used for swimming towards food or away from harm 4 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JjUfNkRprGE
Bacterial shapes • Cocci : spheres (e.g., Staphylococcus) • Bacilli : rods (e.g., E. coli) • Spirilla and spirochetes: spirals • Arrangements: pairs, chains, clusters 5

Procedure for Gram staining Primary stain — crystal violet Flood the smear with crystal violet for 1 minute. Rinse Wash gently with tap water. Mordant — Gram’s iodine Cover with Gram’s iodine for 1 minute. Iodine combines with crystal violet to form the crystal violet– iodine (CV–I) complex. At this stage, all bacteria appear dark violet. Rinse and drain Wash with tap water and remove excess water from the slide. Decolorize Apply the decolorizer (95% ethanol or an ethanol–acetone mixture) briefly Rinse immediately; counterstain Immediately rinse with running water. Cover with safranin for 1 minute, then wash with tap water. Safranin stains cells that were decolorized. Air-dry Allow the smear to dry at room temperature. Examine microscopically Examine using the low-power and high-power objectives, then the oil-immersion objective. Expected result: Gram-positive — purple | Gram-negative — pink/red

Gram stain • Developed by Hans Christian Gram in 1884 • Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan wall, stains purple • Gram-negative: thin wall plus outer membrane, stains pink • Result guides antibiotic choice 7
• Look at the stained image • Decide: Gram-positive or Gram-negative? • Which feature of the wall explains the colour? 8
Classification of bacteria • Shape and motility • Gram stain • Temperature: psychrophiles, mesophiles, thermophiles, hyperthermophiles • Oxygen: obligate aerobes, obligate anaerobes, facultative 11

How bacteria cause disease • Pathogenicity: the ability of a microbe to cause disease • A pathogen must enter, attach, grow, evade and damage • Host-pathogen interaction is a two-sided contest • Virulence factors are the tools that tip the balance 12
Adherence • Adherence (attachment) is essential for colonising a new host • Needs two partners: a receptor on the host cell yyand a ligand on the microbe • Ligands: fimbriae or pili, or M protein 13

Experiment 3: Microscopy of Plant Cells and Osmotic Responses 1. Aim To observe cells using a light microscope, identify major cellular features, prepare a wet mount of onion epidermis, and investigate how plant and mammalian cells respond to hypotonic, isotonic, and hypertonic solutions. 2. Learning Objectives Operate a light microscope and observe specimens at increasing magnification. Identify major features of cells from observed specimens or provided images. Prepare and examine a wet mount of onion epidermis. Estimate magnification Explain osmotic water movement and compare the responses of plant cells to different tonicities. 3. Introduction Microscopy allows biologists to observe cells and compare their structures. Plant cells typically have a cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, and a large vacuole; a nucleus may be visible depending on the preparation and stain. Onion epidermis is a useful plant-cell specimen because the epidermal layer is thin and the cells are relatively large. Onion bulb epidermal cells generally do not show obvious green chloroplasts because the bulb is an underground storage organ. The movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane is called osmosis. The direction of net water movement depends on the relative solute concentrations inside and outside a cell. Plant and mammalian cells respond differently because plant cells have a rigid cell wall whereas mammalian cells do not. 4. Materials and Apparatus Light microscope Onion Clean microscope slides and coverslips Forceps and dropper Iodine solution Paper towel or lint-free tissue Hypotonic, isotonic, and hypertonic solutions. PPE: laboratory coat, gloves, and safety goggles 5. Part A — Microscopy and Cell Identification Procedure: Onion epidermal wet mount 1. Quarter the onion and isolate one onion leaf. 2. Break the leaf in half and carefully peel off a thin layer of epidermis. Avoid folding it; use forceps to unfold it if needed. 3. Place the flattened epidermis on a clean microscope slide. 4. Add a small drop of iodine solution to the specimen.

5. Carefully lower a coverslip onto the specimen and use absorbent paper to remove excess iodine. 6. Place the slide on the microscope stage. Begin with the scanning objective (10×) and locate a region that is a single cell layer thick. 7. Switch to the 40× objective and refocus. 8. Observe the cells and draw a representative cell, labelling the structures that can be distinguished. 6. Part B — Response of Plant Cells to Tonicity Observe and record how plant cells respond in hypotonic, isotonic, and hypertonic solutions. Solution Expected water movement Typical plant-cell response Hypotonic Net water enters the cell Cell swells and becomes turgid; the cell wall limits expansion. Isotonic No net water movement No major net change in cell volume; the cell may be less turgid than in a hypotonic solution. Hypertonic Net water leaves the cell The protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall; this is called plasmolysis. 7. Observations and Drawings In your notebook or in the space provided, draw and label: One plant cell observed by you. Plant cells in hypotonic, isotonic, and hypertonic solutions. For each cell drawing, label the major features visible and include an approximate scale bar where required. Plant cell________________________________________________________________________________ Plant-cell response to tonicity _______________________________________________________________________ 8. Results and Conclusion Summarize the cellular features observed in the plant specimens. State how plant cells responded to hypotonic, isotonic, and hypertonic conditions 9. Precautions Prepare a thin, flat onion epidermal layer to reduce overlapping cells. Lower the coverslip gently to minimize air bubbles. Begin focusing with the lowest objective and use fine focus at high magnification. Handle glass slides, coverslips, forceps, and iodine carefully. Use only instructor-provided slides and solutions; follow laboratory biosafety instructions. 10. Experiment 10: Gene amplification by Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) Aim To amplify a specific DNA fragment using the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) technique. Introduction Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is an in vitro molecular biology technique used to amplify a specific DNA sequence, producing millions of copies from a small quantity of starting DNA. PCR was developed by Kary B. Mullis in 1983, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993. The technique has revolutionized biological research and is widely used in genetic engineering, molecular diagnostics, forensic science, and clinical research. PCR requires template DNA, two sequence-specific oligonucleotide primers, deoxyribonucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs), a thermostable DNA polymerase, and an appropriate reaction buffer. The amplification process takes place in a thermal cycler through three major steps: 1. Denaturation: The reaction mixture is heated to approximately 95°C to separate double-stranded DNA into single strands. 2. Annealing: The temperature is lowered to 50-65°C to allow forward and reverse primers to bind to their complementary sequences on the template DNA. 3. Extension: The temperature is raised to approximately 72°C, allowing Taq DNA polymerase to extend the primers by incorporating dNTPs and synthesizing new DNA strands. These steps are repeated for multiple cycles, resulting in exponential amplification of the target DNA sequence. Components of PCR and Their Functions:

Component Function Template DNA Contains the target gene to be amplified. Forward and reverse primers Define the region of DNA to be amplified. dNTPs Building blocks required for DNA synthesis. Taq DNA polymerase Catalyses the synthesis of new DNA strands. MgSO₄ Provides Mg²⁺ ions, an essential cofactor for DNA polymerase. PCR buffer Maintains suitable pH and ionic conditions for enzyme activity. Sterile Milli-Q water Adjusts the final reaction volume. Materials and Equipment Required Reagents: • Template DNA* • Forward and reverse oligonucleotide primers • dNTP mix • Taq DNA polymerase • 10× ThermoPol buffer • MgSO₄ solution • Sterile Milli-Q water Equipment: • PCR tubes • Micropipettes and sterile tips • Microcentrifuge • Ice bucket • Thermal cycler *the template DNA used was a 1,593bp fragment of PKM2 protein gene. Experimental Procedure

A. Preparation of PCR Reaction Mixture The following reagents are used to prepare a 50 µL PCR reaction: Component Volume Sterile Milli-Q water 35.5 µL 10× ThermoPol buffer 5 µL 100mM MgSO₄ 1 µL 10mM dNTP mix 2 µL 10µM Forward primer 2 µL 10µM Reverse primer 2 µL Template DNA 2 µL Taq DNA polymerase .5 µL Total volume 50 µL B. PCR Amplification 1. Thaw the reagents and keep them on ice during reaction preparation. 2. Label the PCR tube appropriately. 3. Add the required volumes of reagents according to the reaction composition. 4. Mix gently and briefly centrifuge the tube to collect the reaction mixture at the bottom. 5. Place the PCR tube in the thermal cycler. 6. Set the following amplification programme: PCR amplification programme: Step Temperature Time Initial denaturation 95°C 1 min Denaturation 95°C 30 sec Annealing 57°C 30 sec Extension 72°C 1 min Number of cycles 35 cycles Final extension 72°C 5 min Hold 4°C Until collection

7. After completion of the programme, collect the PCR products. 8. Store the amplified products at −20°C until further analysis or proceed directly to agarose gel electrophoresis. Expected Outcome Amplification of the target gene: a 1,593bp fragment of PKM2 protein gene. The amplified product will be analysed by agarose gel electrophoresis to determine the presence and approximate size of the DNA fragment.
